prompt: A team's integration stage runs 200 tests on unchanged `main` and goes red on roughly two runs in three. Each time a different test fails, and it passes when re-run. Measured individually, each test fails only about once in 200 runs. What is the best diagnosis and response?

options.text: Each test is 99.5 % reliable, so most red runs must be genuine regressions; revert the latest merges
options.explanation: 0.5 % is a per-test rate. The code is unchanged, and the failing test differs each time and passes on re-run, which is the signature of flakiness rather than a regression.

options.text: Configure the stage to retry until it goes green, since flaky failures are harmless noise
options.explanation: Blind retries hide flakiness, and an intermittent failure can be a real defect such as a race condition, which would then ship.

options.text: Rare per-test flakes compound across 200 tests, because a run is red if any one fails. Track flakiness per test, quarantine the worst with an owner, and investigate them for real races
options.explanation: Correct. With 200 independent chances of a 0.5 % flake, all tests pass together only about 37 % of the time. Quarantine with an owner restores trust while keeping the repair work visible.

options.text: The chances add up to 200 × 0.5 % = 100 %, so every run should be red; the CI system must be miscounting
options.explanation: Probabilities of separate events do not simply add. The chance that every test passes is 0.995 multiplied by itself 200 times, about 0.37, so about 63 % of runs are red, matching what the team sees.

workedExample:
1. Symptoms: unchanged code, a different failing test each time, passes on re-run. That points to flaky tests, not a regression.
2. Why so many red runs? One test passes 99.5 % of the time. All 200 pass together only if each one does: 0.995 multiplied by itself 200 times, about 0.37.
3. So about 63 % of runs go red on correct code, roughly two in three, as observed. This assumes independent flakes; real flakes are often correlated, so treat it as a model.
4. Response: record flakiness per test, quarantine the worst offenders out of the blocking suite with an owner and a ticket, and fix them. Look for timing, ordering, shared-state and network causes, and for genuine races.
5. Do not paper over it with automatic retries: Google reported that about 84 % of observed pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test, and that people learn to ignore failures from noisy tests.

link.title: Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them
